title: Seekers
hookLine: Benedict XVI created a space for dialogue with non-believers

cards: Some families have one person who doesn't fit the usual boxes. Not religious, exactly. Not hostile either.

They'll come to midnight Mass at Christmas and stand at the back. They read about the stars late at night and wonder what any of it is for. Ask what they believe and they'll say, honestly, I don't know.
Today's neighbor may have no faith at all, and a pope once asked the Church to make room for exactly this person. Today, seekers.

teach.h: A COURTYARD FOR THOSE WHO WERE NOT JEWS.
teach.b: Pope Benedict XVI, speaking to the officials who work alongside him in Rome, reached back to the temple in Jerusalem. It had an outer courtyard, he recalled, where people who were not Jews could come close.

teach.h: ROOM FOR THOSE TO WHOM GOD IS UNKNOWN.
teach.b: The Church needs something like that today, he suggested: a place for people to whom God is unknown, and who still don't want to be left simply without God.
A place to come close, ask their questions, and be taken seriously.

teach.h: AN OPEN GATE, NOT A DEBATE STAGE.
teach.b: A courtyard, not a debate stage: open air, an open gate, room to walk in and walk out.

A Vatican office for culture later took up the name, holding public gatherings where believers and non-believers talked about art, science, meaning and death. Behind the idea are words from the Gospel.
In Matthew, Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Ask, and it shall be given you: seek, and you shall find: knock, and it shall be opened to you."
Some readers hear in it a promise for people still looking, not only for those who have arrived.
In Acts, in the Athens scene from day five hundred fifty-one, Paul tells the crowd that God made people so that they would seek him, and that he is not far from any one of us.

teach.h: KNOCK, AND IT SHALL BE OPENED TO YOU.
teach.b: In these texts, seeking is something to honor, not something to fix in one conversation. The question for the courtyard isn't how fast someone gets inside.
It's whether they find the gate open, and someone willing to listen.

how: A Vatican office for culture has hosted public gatherings, known as the Courtyard of the Gentiles, where believers and non-believers discuss questions of meaning together. In parishes, some Catholics host open discussion groups or simply spend time listening to friends who do not believe.

games.q: a friend says, honestly, "I don't know if God exists, but I can't stop wondering." what does the courtyard idea suggest?
o: hand them an argument and wait for agreement.
listen, take the question seriously, and leave the gate open.
change the subject, since they aren't a believer.
games.why: Benedict XVI pictured a place where people to whom God is unknown can come close and be taken seriously: an open courtyard, not a debate.

practice: Let one person come to mind who doesn't believe, or isn't sure, or has stopped, and recall a question they've asked, or might ask, about God, or suffering, or why anyone bothers with church.

Don't plan an answer; plan to listen, and rehearse letting them finish every sentence. If you pray, you can hold them before God without any agenda; if you don't, simply wish them well in their searching.

wordCard.voice: Seekers. People still looking, for whom Benedict XVI asked the Church to open something like the temple's outer courtyard. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: seek, spoken to many at once, in Matthew 7:7 — seek, and you shall find.

carryVoice: Your line: the courtyard. An open gate, and someone willing to hear the question. That's today, done.
